# What telltale checks

telltale has three kinds of check:

1. **Changes since the snapshot**, when there is one: every difference
   between the machine now and the known-good snapshot, with changes that a
   signed package update explains set apart. See
   [how it works](how-it-works.md).
2. **The hardening checklist** below: settings any well-run machine should
   have.
3. **Suspicious on any machine**, below: things worth a look whether or not
   there is a snapshot.

Package-owned files are also checked against the distribution's signed
packages (see [how it works](how-it-works.md)).

Every finding has a severity. From the highest:

- **tampering**: a checklist item that passed in the snapshot and fails now
  (the regression rule), something the machine's own tools hide, or a
  system file that does not match its signed package;
- **backdoor sign**: something that gives someone a way in or hides one;
- **weak setting**: a setting that should be stricter;
- **note**: worth knowing, not a problem by itself.

Every finding in a report also carries its ID (for `telltale accept` and
the web UI's exceptions), the evidence, and the exact command that would
fix it on that machine. telltale never runs a fix itself.

## The hardening checklist

44 items. A failing item is a weak setting. An item that passed in the known-good snapshot and fails now is raised to tampering, because attackers loosen these settings to keep a way back in. An item whose input could not be read (most need root) is listed as skipped, never guessed. References are to the DISA STIG for Ubuntu 22.04 where a rule applies; the other items are telltale's own.

### SSH server

- **TT-SSH-001** SSH root login is off (key login from the telltale server only).
  If root may log in over SSH, anyone who learns the root password or plants a root key gets straight in as root. The only exception expected is key login from the telltale server's own address.
- **TT-SSH-002** SSH refuses accounts with empty passwords.
  With this on, an account that has no password can be logged into over the network by anyone who knows its name. *STIG V-260526 (UBTU-22-255025).*
- **TT-SSH-003** SSH password login is noted (key-only login is stronger).
  Password login lets attackers guess passwords over the network; key-only login does not. This is noted, not failed, because many machines rely on it.
- **TT-SSH-004** SSH X11 forwarding is off.
  X11 forwarding lets a logged-in session reach back into the user's desktop, and is rarely needed on a server. *STIG V-260529 (UBTU-22-255040).*
- **TT-SSH-005** SSH allows at most 4 login attempts per connection.
  More attempts per connection make password guessing faster.
- **TT-SSH-006** SSH host-based login is off.
  Host-based login trusts other machines to vouch for users, so taking over one machine opens this one.
- **TT-SSH-007** SSH ignores .rhosts files.
  A .rhosts file lets a user grant password-free access from other machines; attackers drop one to get back in.
- **TT-SSH-008** sshd configuration files are mode 0644 or stricter and owned by root.
  Anyone who can write the SSH server configuration can let themselves in, for example by turning root login back on.
- **TT-SSH-009** No sshd Match block loosens a checked setting.
  A Match block can quietly turn root login or empty passwords back on for chosen users or addresses while the global settings look hardened. Only the telltale server's own block (key login for root from its address) is expected.
- **TT-SSH-010** SSH ignores users' environment files.
  With this on, a user's ~/.ssh/environment can set LD_PRELOAD and similar variables for their sessions, a known way to run hidden code. *STIG V-260526 (UBTU-22-255025).*
- **TT-SSH-011** SSH checks the permissions of users' key files.
  Without this check, sshd accepts authorized_keys files that other users can write, so anyone can add their own key.

### Accounts

- **TT-ACCT-001** Only root has UID 0.
  Any account with UID 0 is root under another name, a classic hidden way back in.
- **TT-ACCT-002** No account has an empty password.
  An account with an empty password can be logged into by anyone who knows its name. *STIG V-260571 (UBTU-22-611065).*
- **TT-ACCT-003** System accounts have no login shell.
  Service accounts (UID below 1000) never need to log in; giving one a shell is a quiet way to add a login nobody watches. *STIG V-288817 (UBTU-22-412040).*
- **TT-ACCT-004** Passwords are hashed with yescrypt or SHA-512.
  Older hashes (MD5, DES, SHA-256) can be cracked quickly by anyone who gets a copy of /etc/shadow.

### sudo

- **TT-SUDO-001** No sudo rule skips the password (NOPASSWD).
  A NOPASSWD rule turns anyone who gets into that account, even without its password, into root. Before removing it, give each account it covers a password, or nobody may be able to become root. *STIG V-274860 (UBTU-22-432011).*
- **TT-SUDO-002** sudo always asks for authentication (no !authenticate).
  A Defaults !authenticate line makes sudo hand out root without asking for any password. *STIG V-260558 (UBTU-22-432010).*
- **TT-SUDO-003** sudoers files are mode 0440 and owned by root.
  Anyone who can write a sudoers file can give themselves root.

### File permissions

- **TT-FILE-001** /etc/shadow is mode 0640 or stricter, owned by root, group shadow.
  /etc/shadow holds the password hashes; anyone who can read it can try to crack them offline, and anyone who can write it can set any password.
- **TT-FILE-002** /etc/passwd is mode 0644 or stricter and owned by root.
  Anyone who can write /etc/passwd can add an account with UID 0.
- **TT-FILE-003** /etc/group is mode 0644 or stricter and owned by root.
  Anyone who can write /etc/group can add themselves to the sudo or shadow group.
- **TT-FILE-004** /etc/gshadow is mode 0640 or stricter, owned by root, group shadow.
  /etc/gshadow holds group passwords and administrators; write access lets someone join any group.
- **TT-FILE-005** No world-writable files in system paths.
  A world-writable program, library or config file in a system path can be replaced by any local user, and root will run their version. *STIG V-260485 (UBTU-22-232010), STIG V-260486 (UBTU-22-232015), STIG V-260487 (UBTU-22-232020), STIG V-260513 (UBTU-22-232145).*
- **TT-FILE-006** cron directories are mode 0700 and owned by root.
  Readable cron directories show attackers which jobs run as root; writable ones let them add their own.

### Firewall

- **TT-FW-001** A firewall is active.
  Without a firewall, every service that listens on the network can be reached, including one an attacker starts. *STIG V-260516 (UBTU-22-251020).*

### Kernel settings

- **TT-KERN-001** Memory layout randomisation is fully on.
  Randomising where programs and libraries sit in memory makes many exploits fail. *STIG V-260474 (UBTU-22-213020).*
- **TT-KERN-002** setuid programs do not dump core.
  A core dump of a setuid program can contain password hashes or keys that an ordinary user can then read.
- **TT-KERN-003** Kernel addresses are hidden from users.
  Kernel addresses help an attacker aim a kernel exploit, for example one used to load a rootkit.
- **TT-KERN-004** Only root can read the kernel log.
  The kernel log reveals addresses and hardware details that help an attacker aim an exploit. *STIG V-260472 (UBTU-22-213010).*
- **TT-KERN-005** ICMP redirects are ignored.
  Accepting redirects lets someone on the network reroute this machine's traffic through themselves.
- **TT-KERN-006** ICMP redirects are not sent.
  Only a router needs to send redirects; on other machines it helps an attacker who has taken over the network path.
- **TT-KERN-007** Source-routed packets are refused.
  Source routing lets a sender choose the path of a packet, which helps get past firewalls.
- **TT-KERN-008** TCP SYN cookies are on.
  SYN cookies keep the machine reachable during a SYN flood. *STIG V-260522 (UBTU-22-253010).*
- **TT-KERN-009** Symlink protection is on.
  Without it, a local user can plant symlinks in shared directories such as /tmp that trick root into overwriting files.
- **TT-KERN-010** Hard link protection is on.
  Without it, a local user can hard-link files they do not own, such as /etc/shadow, into places root later writes or exposes.
- **TT-KERN-011** IPv6 ICMP redirects are ignored.
  Accepting redirects lets someone on the network reroute this machine's IPv6 traffic through themselves.
- **TT-KERN-012** Processes cannot trace unrelated processes.
  With unrestricted ptrace, any program a user runs can read the memory of their other programs, such as SSH agents and password prompts.

### Services

- **TT-SVC-001** No telnet server is installed.
  Telnet sends passwords in clear text and is a common way back in once installed. *STIG V-260483 (UBTU-22-215035).*
- **TT-SVC-002** No rsh or rlogin server is installed.
  rsh and rlogin send everything in clear text and can trust other machines without a password. *STIG V-260482 (UBTU-22-215030).*
- **TT-SVC-003** No TFTP server is installed.
  TFTP has no authentication at all; anyone who can reach it can read, and often write, its files.
- **TT-SVC-004** No NIS packages are installed.
  NIS shares account data over the network without encryption, including password hashes.
- **TT-SVC-005** auditd is installed.
  The audit daemon records logins, privilege use and changes to key files, the trail you need after a break-in. *STIG V-260590 (UBTU-22-653010).*
- **TT-SVC-006** AppArmor is enabled.
  AppArmor confines services to what they need, so a compromised service cannot freely read or change the rest of the system. *STIG V-260557 (UBTU-22-431015).*
- **TT-SVC-007** Security updates install automatically (unattended-upgrades).
  Most break-ins use holes that already have a fix; installing security updates automatically closes them without waiting for someone to remember.

## Suspicious on any machine

25 kinds of finding, under 17 IDs. These need no snapshot. The finding key (the ID a report shows for each finding) starts as given here and ends with the account, path or program it is about.

- **TT-HEUR-001** An account other than root has user id 0. *Backdoor sign.*
  User id 0 is root, whatever the account is called. A second account with id 0 is a classic hidden way back in: it logs in as root under another name.
  Key: `heur.uid0:`
- **TT-HEUR-002** An account has an empty password. *Weak setting.*
  Wherever password logins are allowed, anyone can log in as that account without knowing anything. Shown only when the password could be read, which usually needs root.
  Key: `heur.empty_password:`
- **TT-HEUR-003** A system account has a login shell. *Note.*
  Accounts that run services should not be able to log in. A shell on one can be a quiet way back in.
  Key: `heur.system_shell:`
- **TT-HEUR-004** /etc/ld.so.preload exists. *Backdoor sign.*
  Every program on the machine loads the libraries it lists. Userland rootkits use it to hide files, processes and connections from the machine's own tools.
  Key: `heur.ld_preload`
- **TT-HEUR-005** A program runs from a temporary or hidden place, or was deleted while running. *Backdoor sign.*
  Software that belongs on a machine is installed in system directories and stays on disk. Programs running from /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, a hidden directory or a deleted file are typical of malware. A note when the program sits in a hidden directory in its own user's home (developer tools such as ~/.vscode-server do that); a backdoor sign everywhere else.
  Key: `heur.proc_exe:`
- **TT-HEUR-005** A program still runs the version from before a package upgrade. *Note.*
  Its file was replaced by an upgrade while it ran: the deleted file was the old version, and the file now at that path belongs to a package and is newer than the process. Restart it to run the new version.
  Key: `heur.stale_exe:`
- **TT-HEUR-006** An SSH key forces a command. *Backdoor sign.*
  A command= option in authorized_keys runs a fixed program on every login with that key. It can hide a backdoor behind a key that looks harmless. The telltale server's own key is recognised and never reported.
  Key: `heur.forced_command`
- **TT-HEUR-007** A key lets root log in over SSH. *Note.*
  Listed so you can check every key that gives root access. The telltale server's own key is recognised. With a snapshot these notes are left out, and keys added since the snapshot are reported from the comparison instead, as backdoor signs.
  Key: `heur.root_key`
- **TT-HEUR-008** A setuid or setgid program belongs to no package. *Backdoor sign.*
  A setuid program runs with its owner's rights, often root's, whoever starts it. One that no package installed may be a planted root shell. A note under /usr/local, where people install their own programs.
  Key: `heur.unowned_setuid:`
- **TT-HEUR-008** A program with file capabilities belongs to no package. *Backdoor sign.*
  File capabilities give a program part of root's power (reading any file, raw network access) without the setuid bit. One that no package installed may be a planted way to escalate. A note under /usr/local.
  Key: `heur.unowned_caps:`
- **TT-HEUR-008** An exact copy of a package's setuid program sits elsewhere. *Note.*
  It grants nothing the original does not, but check that you made the copy.
  Key: `heur.setuid_packaged_copy:`
- **TT-HEUR-009** A file is marked immutable or append-only. *Backdoor sign.*
  These flags stop even root from changing or deleting a file. Attackers set them to protect a backdoor from removal; ordinary systems rarely set them on system files.
  Key: `heur.immutable:`
- **TT-HEUR-010** A loaded kernel module comes from no installed package. *Backdoor sign.*
  Code in the kernel can hide anything from anything running on the machine. Modules built locally (DKMS drivers, for example) also show here; accept them once you have checked them.
  Key: `heur.module:`
- **TT-HEUR-011** A program that no package installed listens on a port. *Note.*
  A backdoor often waits for connections. Listed so you can check each one; ports of the same program are grouped.
  Key: `heur.unowned_listener:`
- **TT-HEUR-012** The machine's own tools hide something telltale can see. *Tampering.*
  telltale reads /proc, /proc/net and the filesystem itself and compares what it finds with what ps, ss, ls and lsmod print. A process, port, file or module that it sees and a tool leaves out is strong evidence of a rootkit.
  Key: `heur.crossview:`
- **TT-HEUR-013** A startup link leads outside the system directories. *Backdoor sign.*
  A cron job, systemd unit or other startup file that is a symbolic link into /tmp, a home or another place outside /usr, /lib and /etc runs whatever is put there. Linking a unit in from /var/tmp is a known trick. Links are followed as the kernel follows them, not as their text reads. A weak setting when the link masks a security service (auditd, AppArmor, ufw, nftables, fail2ban) by pointing it at /dev/null.
  Key: `heur.persist_link:`
- **TT-HEUR-013** A startup link runs a package's own file outside the system directories. *Note.*
  Some vendors do this (Chrome links a daily cron job into /opt). The file it runs is still checked against its package, and a file that does not match is reported on its own.
  Key: `heur.persist_link_pkg:`
- **TT-HEUR-013** A startup link points at a file that does not exist. *Note.*
  Nothing runs now, but whoever can create the missing file decides what runs next.
  Key: `heur.persist_link_dangling:`
- **TT-HEUR-013** A user's own systemd unit starts at login. *Note.*
  Enabled with systemctl --user. Listed with the command it runs, so you can check it; its contents are judged like any other startup file.
  Key: `heur.user_unit:`
- **TT-HEUR-014** A system file is diverted by hand, or by a package that is not installed. *Backdoor sign.*
  A dpkg diversion makes package updates install their copy of a file under another name, so the file at the original path is never replaced and is not the packaged one. It is a way to keep a replaced system program in place. A note for exactly the diversions Ubuntu's own minimised images make (/usr/bin/man and /sbin/initctl), on Ubuntu.
  Key: `heur.local_diversion:`
- **TT-HEUR-015** A startup file connects out, or downloads code and runs it. *Backdoor sign.*
  A cron job, unit, shell start-up file or similar that opens a reverse shell (/dev/tcp, nc -e, socat exec:, a scripting one-liner) or pipes a download into a shell is the commonest persistence there is. Accepting it covers only the lines seen; a new matching line is a finding again.
  Key: `heur.persist_callback:`
- **TT-HEUR-016** A PAM module used at login belongs to no package. *Backdoor sign.*
  PAM modules run inside every login and see every password typed. One that no package installed may record passwords or let a secret password in.
  Key: `heur.pam_unowned:`
- **TT-HEUR-016** A PAM module name climbs out of the module directory. *Backdoor sign.*
  A name with .. in it makes PAM load a library from somewhere else, where no package check looks.
  Key: `heur.pam_path_escape:`
- **TT-HEUR-016** The PAM configuration names a module that is not on the machine. *Note.*
  Usually left over from a removed package. Whoever can create the file decides what runs at login.
  Key: `heur.pam_missing:`
- **TT-HEUR-017** A user's systemd unit directory holds more than telltale reads. *Note.*
  Anyone can fill their own unit directory. telltale reads at most 2,000 entries and 8 MiB of text from one user's directory, and 64 MiB from all users' together, so that no user can make a scan run out of memory or time. What lies past that was not read, and a unit hidden there was not seen. Thousands of files in such a directory are themselves unusual: look at what fills it.
  Key: `heur.persist_flooded:`
